messages.body_plain:
Yes, I expect this will crash lots of systems.  Comments below

On Sun, Jul 31, 2011 at 7:14 AM, Paul Menzel
<paule...@users.sourceforge.net> wrote:
> Dear plyr folks,
>
>
> I am sorry for this noob question and I promise I am currently reading
> up on plyr’s features and usage. I read the announcement of plyr 1.6 on
> the r-help list and I was wondering if plyr could help me.
>
> I need to simulate how long a iterated random walk stays negativ [1].
> Therefore I want to simulate a lot of (very long) random walks and look
> when they cross 0. The code currently looks basically like this for a
> normal random walk.
>
>        f1 <- function(n = 100000, # number of simulations
>                       length = 100000) # length of iterated sum
>        {
>           z0 = 0L
>           z = rep(0L, times=length/2)
>
>           for (j in 1:n) {
>                   x = sample(c(-1L, 1L), size=length, replace=TRUE)
>                   if (x[1] >= 0 ) {
>                           z0 = z0 + 1L
>                           next
>                   }
>
>                   s = cumsum(x)
>                   for (i in 1:length-1) {
>                           if (s[i] < 0 && s[i + 1] >= 0) {
>                                   z[i/2] = z[i/2] + 1L
>                                   break
>                           }
>                   }
>           }
>           c(z0, z)
>        }
>
> On r-help [1] it was suggested to use more vectorization to avoid the
> for loops.
>

You will get the hang of this with some practice.  You are trying to
accumulate too much data.

Re-design this so you efficiently conduct 1 (as in one!) simulation,
collect the information you need, and then conduct the next one.  Then
worry about looping later.  To my eye, you do not need plyr, you just
need a regular old R lapply or sapply to get this done.

runOneSimulation <- function(x,y,z){
     ## figure out how long cumsum stays negative
    res
}

This returns "res", the number of periods the sum is negative.

Once that works well, then it is easy to iterate.  Hell, even a for
loop will suffice.  You want to avoid idioms like

c(z0, z)

Because it calls a memory expanding operation over and over.  Instead,
allocate the memory and fill it in.

How to do runOneSimulation  efficiently?  I think we would have to do
some testiing, the efficient approach will depend on the most likely
scenario.  Your approach here allocates a giant vector, even if your
sum runs positive and the simulation stops.  I would not do that.

I don't really think cumsum is the best way because it presupposes you
allocate that giant vector.  I'm doing some testing. How about this.
It is not "vectorized", but it runs fast on my system and clarity is a
plus.

##Paul Johnson
## Aug. 4, 2011

## for R question about "how long does a sum of random
## walk stay negative

runOneSimulation <- function(){
   counter <- 0
   mysum <- 0
   while (mysum <= 0){
      mysum <- mysum + runif(1, min= -1,max= 1)
      counter <- counter + 1
      if (counter > 10000) break
    }
   #print(counter) ##testing
   #print(mysum)  ##testing
   counter
}

set.seed(123123)
##test
runOneSimulation()
nsim <- 50000
myres <- numeric(nsim)

for ( i in 1:nsim){
   myres[i] <- runOneSimulation()
 }

hist(myres)

> The problem when removing the outer for loop is, that when simulating
> for example a million random walks with a length of one million the
> matrix does not fit into the RAM and my system even freezes [2].
>
> So I could do some basic calculations to look how much free memory the
> system has only do that much samples of random walks of a certain length
> so that they fit into memory, save the result and let a script call this
> over and over again until I have the wanted amount of simulations.
>
> Reading about plyr I understand it was written just for this purpose.
> That means it splits the original data/matrix and processes small

messages.body_plain:
hey all

i'm stuck using colsplit for the most simple case- when the two variable names are concatenated.

consider the following example, where we measure states incidence of growth (y) and interest rates (i) over time. We measure growth twice (in 90 and 92) whilst we only measure interest rates in 90.

rdf        <- data.frame(state = factor(1:4),
                           y90 = c(1, 2, 1, 2),
                           y92 = c(2, 1, 2, 1),
                           i90 = c(3, 3, 3, 3))
> rdf

  state y90 y92 i90
1     1   1   2   3
2     2   2   1   3
3     3   1   2   3
4     4   2   1   3

Melting is simple, but we get the problem of not having a separate indicator for year

rdfm <-melt(rdf, id = 1)

> rdfm
   state variable value
1      1      y90     1
2      2      y90     2
3      3      y90     1
4      4      y90     2
5      1      y92     2
6      2      y92     1
7      3      y92     2
8      4      y92     1
9      1      i90     3
10     2      i90     3
11     3      i90     3
12     4      i90     3

clearly, it's required that we separate the second column, so we can have a year and a variable type indicator. That is:

   state year variable value
1      1   90        y     1
2      2   90        y     2

but the following

rdfm2 <- cbind(rdfm, colsplit(rdfm$variable, names = c("variable", "year")))

just provides this error

Error in is.character(pattern) : 'pattern' is missing

what "pattern" does colsplit require for conatenated names?

Thanks!

messages.body_plain:
Hi:

The problem is that colsplit() needs a character on which to split the
strings, just like the strsplit() function in base. It is much easier
to perform the column split if you add a character between the first
and second positions of the original strings:

library('reshape')

rdf <- data.frame(state = factor(1:4),

                  y_90 = c(1, 2, 1, 2),
                  y_92 = c(2, 1, 2, 1),
                  i_90 = c(3, 3, 3, 3))
rdfm <- melt(rdf, id = 1)
cbind(rdfm[, -2], colsplit(rdfm$variable, split = '_',

                           names = c('variable', 'year')))

The default split string is "", but since you have three characters in
the variable names, that's not what you want here.

HTH,
Dennis

Hi:

Here's an example - I have no idea how close it is to your situation

DF <- data.frame(f1 = sample(letters[1:3], 200, replace = TRUE),

library('plyr')

# Sort by decreasing values of A
arrange(dcast(DF, f1 ~ f2, value_var = 'y', fun = length), desc(A))
  f1  A  B  C

2  b 22 19 24
3  a 21 19 27

  f1  A  B  C
1  c 24 22 22
2  a 21 19 27
3  b 22 19 24

arrange() is in the plyr package, and is a replacement function of
sorts for order() with respect to columns of a data frame.

defined at the midpoint of the two middle samples, even if no single

groups.)

ddply(diamonds, .(color), with, quantile(price, .85))
